endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Define and document which systems, APIs, and data sources an agentic AI system is authorized to query — this is the agentic equivalent of a training data inventory.

endorsements.title: Reimagining psychiatric care with agentic AI: promise, challenges, and a roadmap forward
endorsements.quote: For any system that interacts with patients, it is also essential to measure escalation behavior and safety overrides, that is how reliably the system routes high-risk situations to human care and what happens after escalation rather than assuming safe behavior from design alone.

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations in Personal Health Large Language Models
endorsements.quote: Escalation triggers are prospectively specified in system logic rather than left to user discretion, because users may not recognize when a query exceeds safe self-management boundaries.

endorsements.title: Medical AI Agents for Clinical Decision Support: Viewpoint Using the Planning, Action, Reflection, and Memory (PARM) Analytical Lens
endorsements.quote: Confidence scores and uncertainty estimates should trigger mandatory human review when agents encounter unusual situations.

evidence.title: ETHOS: Towards a Modular Ethics Framework for Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
evidence.outcome: Appropriate abstention by agentic system when safe recommendations cannot be supported
evidence.effect: ETHOS appropriately increased abstention when safe recommendations could not be supported; no numbers in abstract.
evidence.quote: Results show that ETHOS improves decision reliability by detecting incomplete, inconsistent, or out-of-scope evidence and appropriately increasing abstention when safe recommendations cannot be supported.

evidence.title: Hard to Halt: Automation Bias in Agent-Driven Sequencing Prior Authorization Workflows
evidence.outcome: Agent withholding of prior authorization submission for deficient patient profiles
evidence.effect: Task completion: Gemini 3 Pro 95.45%, Claude Opus 4.5 93.67%, Gemini 3 Flash 56.05%. Larger models nearly universally failed to withhold submission for deficient profiles; Flash withheld 17.33%.
evidence.quote: Larger models achieved much higher task completion rates (Gemini 3 Pro 95.45%, Claude Opus 4.5 93.67%) compared to Gemini 3 Flash (56.05%), but nearly universally failed to withhold submission for deficient profiles whereas Gemini 3 Flash ironically demonstrated superior withholding performance (17.33%).

commentary.bottom_line: One simulated study reports that an agentic system abstained more often when it could not support a safe recommendation, but it gives no numbers, and no study has tested pause or escalation rules in live clinical use. A separate benchmark shows that larger models rarely withheld action on deficient cases, which suggests the hazard is real and that escalation conditions may need to be defined and tested rather than assumed.

perspectives.view: One level 4 offline study tests the practice and reports that ETHOS increased abstention when safe recommendations could not be supported. The abstract gives no numbers, sample size, or comparator. Serious risk of bias, indirectness from simulation, and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

In 836 synthetic prior authorization records, Gemini 3 Pro and Claude Opus 4.5 completed 95.45% and 93.67% of tasks yet nearly always submitted deficient profiles. Gemini 3 Flash withheld 17.33%. High task completion therefore may coexist with failure to stop, so pause conditions likely need direct testing.

Both studies ran offline, and neither reports how escalations reach a human reviewer, how often reviewers act, or what workload results. Commentary sources ask health systems to measure what happens after escalation, and no study here has measured that.

The CHAI playbook rates documentation of the systems, APIs, and data sources an agent may query as a must. That inventory defines the limits of authorized action, but no supplied study tests whether documenting those limits changes agent behavior.

One commentary argues that escalation triggers belong in system logic because patients may not recognize when a question exceeds safe self-care. The benchmark finding that larger models rarely withheld action suggests patients cannot count on an agent to stop on its own and route them to a person.

commentary.research_gap: No study has measured escalation or abstention rules in live clinical workflows. Such studies would need to report how often agents pause or escalate appropriately, the rate of missed escalations, reviewer response time and burden, and patient outcomes after escalation, compared with agents that run without defined stop conditions.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study reports the populations represented, and both used simulated or synthetic data, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Whether escalation triggers work for patients who describe symptoms in other languages or with limited health literacy remains untested.
